problems.title: Unnormalized module rewards do not dominate layer rewards
problems.source_location: arXiv v3, Proposition 2, PDF p.6; conference Eqs.(2),(5), PDF pp.4–5
claim: The comparison maximizes expected squared module/layer gradient gain minus \(\eta^{-1}\) KL to its respective uniform distribution and asserts module-wise objective superiority.
analysis: Take two layers, each containing two scalar modules with gradient \(1\), and \(\eta=1\). Each layer gain is \(2\); each module gain is \(1\). Uniform distributions make the KL penalties zero, so the optimized values are \(V_{\rm layer}=2\), \(V_{\rm module}=1\). More generally the log-sum-exp variational identity and \(a_{ij}\le S_i=\sum_j a_{ij}\) imply \(V_{\rm module}(\eta)\le V_{\rm layer}(\eta)\), reversing the claimed weak ordering. These gradients are realizable in the globally smooth lower-bounded objective \(\sum_{\ell=1}^4(1-\cos\theta_\ell)\) at \(\theta_\ell=\pi/2\).
result: The unnormalized superiority argument is false; it compares different amounts of updated work. The softmax optimizer itself remains valid.
repair: For equal module-count cost, use layer gain \(S_i/K\). Mapping \(q_{ij}=p_i/K\) preserves both this normalized gain and the KL, proving \(K^{-1}V_{\rm layer}(\eta/K)\le V_{\rm module}(\eta)\le V_{\rm layer}(\eta)\). This does not normalize unequal FLOPs or memory.

problems.title: Positive sampling weights need not give positive inclusion
problems.source_location: arXiv v3, Algorithm 1, PDF p.7; analytical algorithm and convergence appendix; weighted_sample_without_replacement
claim: The practical method rejects selections above a parameter budget, while the analytical method samples a module directly and uses different inherited/maximal second moments.
analysis: Use modules with \(3\) and \(1\) parameters out of \(4\), budget fraction \(\delta=1/2\), and objective \(f=1-\cos\theta_1\), initialized at \(\theta_1=\pi/2\) in the larger module. That module’s ratio \(3/4>1/2\) never fits; the smaller module has zero gradient. All updates leave \(\|\nabla f\|^2=1\), despite global smoothness, bounded deterministic unbiased gradient and zero noise variance. Positive nominal probabilities and least-recently-used preferences cannot overcome a hard size exclusion.
result: An unrestricted convergence transfer to the practical budgeted sampler fails. This example does not contradict the analytical algorithm under its own direct-sampling assumptions or identify an excluded block in the reported LLM runs.
repair: Every optimized block must fit, with suitable actual inclusion bounds and optimizer hypotheses, or the target must be restricted to movable parameters. No sufficient replacement practical convergence theorem is established.

problems.title: Repeated bias correction distorts the historical score
claim: The stored recurrence divides its already corrected EMA by \(1-\beta^t\) again at each observation.
analysis: For unit observations and \(\beta=0.8\), the source recurrence gives \(G_1=1\), \(G_2=1/(1-0.8^2)=25/9\), rather than the constant readout \(1\). Two equally strong modules with one and two observations then receive capped squared logits \(1\) and \(5\), hence probabilities approximately \(0.0179862\) and \(0.9820138\). Raw norm smoothing followed by squaring also differs from smoothing squared size-normalized gradients; modules with \(1\) and \(4\) unit-gradient parameters have raw norms \(1,2\) but equal size-normalized norms.
result: The inspected release’s indicator depends on observation count and an unmatched statistic. Its training effect and historical run correspondence remain unestablished.
repair: Store raw \(M_t=\beta M_{t-1}+(1-\beta)x_t\) and compute separate readout \(M_t/(1-\beta^t)\). For constant \(x_t=x\), induction gives readout exactly \(x\). Reconcile the chosen score statistic separately.

problems.title: Backward FLOPs omit input-gradient products
problems.source_location: arXiv v3, Appendix F, PDF pp.42–45; conference Appendix G, PDF pp.41–43
claim: The dense-product convention yields printed quadratic coefficients \(34\) for full backward and \(10\) for frozen backward, in units \(bsh^2\).
analysis: For FFN input width \(h\) and hidden width \(4h\), propagating through the first projection requires \(\nabla Z=(\nabla Z_1\odot{\bf1})W_1^\top\), costing \(8bsh^2\). Q/K/V input gradients contribute another \(6bsh^2\). These products remain necessary in frozen layers above trainable parameters. Adding the missing \(14\) gives full/frozen coefficients \(48\) and \(24\), retaining the source’s other operation conventions. Input gradients may legitimately be pruned below the earliest active layer.
result: Absolute dense-backward counts are incomplete. The qualitative budget threshold can survive the same simplified comparison model; hardware runtime and all graph-pruning cases were not measured.
repair: Include the explicit missing dense products; the resulting counts are \(48bsh^2+8bs^2h+2bas^2+14bsh\) and \(24bsh^2+8bs^2h+2bas^2+14bsh\) under the stated model.
